newsitem.title: USA: PECO plans to buy back debt, shares.
newsitem.headline: PECO plans to buy back debt, shares.

text.p: Officials of PECO Energy Co said the company planned to buy back debt and equity in a 50-50 ratio with proceeds of a proposed $3.6 billion refinancing of its generation-related assets.

The officials also told a news conference the refinancing transaction would involve an offering of 10-year bonds secured by future revenues under a rate structure provided for under a Pennsylvania electricity deregulation law. This would ensure a AAA rating on the instruments, they said.
Issuance of the refinancing bonds was expected to take place around June if the proposal were approved by state regulators, said Tom Hill, PECOs financial vice president.
The interest rate was projected at around 7.25 percent if current interest rates were sustained, Hill said.

PECO President Corbin McNeil said the refinancing transaction, which is aimed at recovering costs that would be lost in a degregulated electricity market, would be the first of its scale in the U.S. utilities industry.
"We are the first utility that we know of to attempt a securitization refinancing of this magnitude," McNeil said.
He said PECO expected to file in April for another $3.5 billion refinancing to recover the remainder of PECO's estimated "stranded costs."
Stranded costs are the difference between the book value of electricity generation-assets and their market value following passage of Pennsylvania's deregulation law last year.
The law is expected to increase rate competition and reduce utilities' ability to recover costs approved by regulators prior to deregulation.

Hill said that by the end of 1998, the book value of PECO's power plants would be $6.5 billion, while the market value would be about $2.6 billion, leaving a total of about $3.9 billion in stranded investments.

In addition, PECO has about $2.6 billion in stranded "regulatory assets," which are essentially costs such as taxes, fuel costs or employee retirment expenses that regulators had required the utility to defer but which it could no longer recover in a deregulated environment.
An additional $600 million in stranded costs would come from unfunded expenses associated with the closure of one nuclear plant and one fossil-fuel plant.

McNeil said the second stage of the refinancing application may be subject to more questioning by the state Public Utilities Commission, and said the first $3.6 billion stage was the amount of stranded costs PECO considered to be beyond debate.
Of the $3.6 billion, $2.4 billion relates to generation capacity and $1.2 billion is in the form of regulatory assets, Hill said.

The second step refinancing would lead to a further reduction averaging about one percent in annual consumer rates, beyond the 2.9 percent projected for the first stage, McNeil said. Once the refinancing bonds were repaid, rates could fall an additional 35 percent absent other factors, he said.
"That will bring our rates down to the competitive marketplace," he said.
